title: The mani sung
hookLine: Om mani padme hum sung in long tunes in Tibetan homes

cards: A pot of butter tea is warming on the stove in a Tibetan kitchen, and the grandmother stirring it is singing under her breath.

The tune is long and slow, rising on one syllable, resting on the next, falling back and starting over. Her grandson, doing homework at the table, hums along without looking up. No drum, no hall, no leader.
Just a melody that has been in this house longer than the stove, and words she has sung all her life: om mani padme hum.

teach.b: Om and hum are sacred syllables without a simple translation; the two middle words are usually translated jewel and lotus. Teachers explain the whole in different ways.
Some link the jewel to compassion and the lotus to wisdom; some take each syllable as its own door. In Tibetan it's often heard as om mani peme hung. Second, whose words.
Tradition ties the mantra to Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion from yesterday's Heart Sutra. In Tibet he is called Chenrezig, and the mani is his.
Saying it calls compassion to mind and wishes it for every being, the stranger as much as the grandchild. Third, sung.

The mani can be murmured on a string of beads, but at home it is also sung, to long tunes that differ from family to family and region to region: while cooking, walking, rocking a baby, sitting with someone who is ill.
A tune can't be hurried. Each syllable stretches, and the breath slows to carry it. Fourth, beyond the voice.
The same words are carved into stones piled along paths, called mani stones.

They're printed on long scrolls packed inside prayer wheels, which people turn clockwise as they walk; tradition says each turn sends the mantra out as if spoken. They're printed on flags so the wind can carry them.
A house, a path, a mountain pass can all be singing the mani at once.

how: Tibetan Buddhists recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, sing it to slow tunes at home and at work, carve it on stones, print it inside prayer wheels that they turn as they walk, and print it on flags.

practice: If you'd like, sing om, mani, padme, hum softly to any slow tune that comes, letting each syllable stretch; families sing it many ways, so there's no melody to get wrong.
If you'd rather not sing these words, hum one long, low note on each out-breath. Either way, while the sound lasts, bring to mind someone who could use a little kindness today.
